parts.subtitle: What Throttle is, how to sign in and get around, and what your role can see.

chapters.title: Welcome to Throttle
chapters.html:
Throttle is the brand team’s work operating system. Anyone in the company asks the brand team for creative work through a request; once approved, that request becomes one or more tasks the brand team works on a board and schedules into sprints. This manual is your self-serve guide to every screen in it.

Request, then task

Request

What someone asks for (a launch pack, a social post, a video). A requester submits it; a lead approves, rejects, or asks for more info. Approving turns it into work.

Task

A unit of work for the brand team, created when a request is approved. Tasks live on the board and move through stages until delivered and done. A big request (a launch pack) becomes several tasks at once.

How a task flows

Every task moves along this path: Backlog → In Sprint → In Progress → In Review → Approved → Delivered → Done. A task can be parked at Ext. Blocked (waiting on something outside the team) or stopped at Abandoned. Two approvals happen along the way, and they are different things:

  • Request approval: a lead approves the incoming request, which creates the task(s).
  • Work approval: a lead approves the deliverable a member submitted (In Review), sending it on to be delivered or marked done.
⚠ Delivered is not Done

Delivered means the work is with the requester for feedback; it becomes Done when the requester accepts it, when it auto-accepts after a set time, or when a lead marks it done. Keep the two approvals straight too: approving a request creates work; approving the work moves a finished task forward.

How to use this manual

Each chapter covers one screen: what it is for, how to read it, and what to do. Jump to the screen you are on using the Contents page or your PDF reader’s bookmarks. Chapters are tagged with the roles that use them:

Requester   Member   Lead   Admin

Callout boxes

✓ Tip

A faster or smarter way to do something.

⚠ Watch out

A common mistake or something easy to misread.

chapters.title: Signing In & Getting Around
chapters.html:
Throttle opens with your work Google account and uses a simple top bar of tabs. This chapter covers signing in and finding your way around.

Signing in

Open throttle.legendoftoys.com and sign in with your @legendoftoys.com Google account. Personal accounts are refused. Signed in, you land on Requests.

The top bar

Throttle uses a horizontal nav across the top (not a sidebar). Which tabs you see depends on your role:

TabVisible to
RequestsEveryone.
BoardMember, Lead, Admin.
SprintsLead, Admin.
DashboardLead, Admin.
SocialEveryone.
SettingsAdmin.

On the right of the bar are a notification bell (for the brand team), your name and role, and Sign out. On the Board and Sprints, press / to open a quick task search.

ⓘ The notification bell

The bell (brand team only) checks every minute for activity in the last 7 days on tasks you are assigned to, excluding your own actions, and shows an unread count. Requesters do not see it. Most screens otherwise load when you open them and refresh after you act, rather than updating on their own.

chapters.title: Roles & What You Can See
chapters.html:
Throttle has four roles, from the people who ask for work to the people who do and manage it. This chapter explains each one and what it can do.

The four roles

Requester

Non-brand staff who submit work requests and review what comes back. They see only Requests and Social, and only their own requests.

Member

Brand team members (designers, copywriters, video, 3D, social). They work tasks on the board: self-assign, move their tasks forward, and submit work for review.

Lead

Brand managers. Everything a member does, plus approving requests, running sprints, approving submitted work, setting priority and owners, and the dashboard.

Admin

Full control, including Settings (managing roles, disciplines and the ageing thresholds that drive auto-accept).

ⓘ Role versus discipline

A person also has a discipline (designer, 3D, copywriter, photo/video, social, lead), set in Settings, which is separate from their role. The role decides what you can do; the discipline describes what kind of work you do. Both are managed by an admin.

Who can move a task

The board only lets you make the moves your role allows; an illegal drag quietly snaps back. In short: members move their own tasks between In Sprint, In Progress, In Review and Ext. Blocked; leads and admins can do everything else (pull from backlog into a sprint, approve work, deliver, mark done, change priority and owners, and abandon).

parts.subtitle: Submitting work, getting it approved, and reviewing what comes back.

chapters.title: Requests
chapters.html:
Requests is where work is asked for and tracked. A requester sees their own requests; a lead or admin sees everything coming in. It is the home screen and the starting point for new work.

What it’s for
Tracking work requests.
Read or act?
Read; launches new requests.
Who
Requester Member Lead Admin
Heading
“My Requests” / “All Requests”.

Reading it

Each request card shows its type, title, status badge, how long it has sat in its current stage, and the created date. Filter with the pills: Needs Action (yours that need a response), All, Pending, Approved, Rejected, Info Needed. Status badges: Pending (yellow), Approved (green), Rejected (red), Info Needed (blue). The time-in-stage chip turns amber after a day and red after two.

Acting on a request

+ New Request starts a new one. A lead or admin also gets an Approval Queue button. On your own cards, contextual buttons appear: Update & Resubmit when a request needs more info, Resubmit when it was rejected, and Delivered: Give Feedback when work is ready for your review.

ⓘ You see what your role allows

Requesters see only their own requests; leads and admins see the whole incoming queue. The “Needs Action” pill is the fastest way for a requester to find a request the brand team has bounced back for more information.

chapters.title: New Request
chapters.html:
New Request is a short wizard for asking the brand team for work. You pick a request type, choose the product if relevant, fill the type’s form, review, and submit.

What it’s for
Submitting a work request.
Read or act?
Action: creates a request.
Who
Requester Member Lead Admin
Steps
Type, product, form, review.

The request types

Pick the type that matches what you need; each has its own tailored form. The ten types are: Launch Pack (a full asset bundle for a new product), Product Creative, Social Media, Advertising, Photo & Video, Copy & Script, Design & Brand, 3D & Motion, Sale Event, and Brand Initiative (internal, brand team only).

Filling it in

  1. Choose the type and, where it applies, the product (some types let you pick several).
  2. Complete the form. Fields vary by type; a title is always required, and some fields only appear based on earlier answers.
  3. Review and submit. A success screen confirms it. Leads will then approve, reject or ask for more info.
⚠ Some types create several tasks

Launch Pack and Sale Event have a checklist, and each ticked item becomes its own task when the request is approved (the screen shows how many). Photo & Video with editing turned on creates two tasks (a shoot and an edit). So one request can spin up a whole batch of work.

chapters.title: Approval Queue
chapters.html:
The Approval Queue is where leads and admins review incoming requests and decide what happens. Approving a request is what turns it into actual tasks for the brand team.

What it’s for
Deciding on incoming requests.
Read or act?
Action: approve / reject / info.
Who
Lead Admin
Creates
Tasks, on approval.

Reviewing a request

The queue lists pending requests oldest first, with a time-in-stage chip (grey, then amber after a day, red after two). Click one to see its full detail: type, title, who submitted it, the products and notes, and all the form fields. Then make a decision:

DecisionWhat it does
ApproveCreates the task(s) and starts the work. A note is optional.
RejectDeclines the request. A note is required, and goes back to the requester.
Need InfoSends it back for more detail. A note is required; the requester can update and resubmit.
ⓘ Approval creates the work

This is the “request approval” step (distinct from approving finished work later on the board). Approving a Launch Pack or Sale Event creates several tasks at once. Reject and Need Info both require a note so the requester knows why.

chapters.title: Giving Feedback
chapters.html:
Giving Feedback is where a requester reviews work the brand team has delivered and either accepts it or asks for a revision. You reach it from the “Delivered: Give Feedback” button on your request.

What it’s for
Accepting or revising delivered work.
Read or act?
Action: accept / request revision.
Who
Requester
Reached from
A delivered request.

Reviewing delivered work

Each delivered task shows the team’s delivery message and the links to the work. For each one you choose Looks good (accept it) or Needs revision (which opens a box for what should change, plus an optional reference link). Submit your feedback for all the delivered tasks at once; the brand team is notified.

⚠ Work auto-accepts if you do nothing

A delivered task shows an “Auto-accepts on [date]” note: if you do not respond by then, it is accepted automatically and marked done. So if something needs changing, choose Needs revision before that date. Asking for a revision sends the task back to the team to rework.

parts.subtitle: The board where work happens, and the sprints that schedule it.

chapters.title: The Board
chapters.html:
The Board is the brand team’s live Kanban of active tasks. Members work their tasks here and leads triage the flow. Clicking any task opens a side panel with everything about it and every action you can take.

What it’s for
Working and tracking tasks.
Read or act?
Action: move and work tasks.
Who
Member Lead Admin
Views
Kanban or Table.

The columns

The Kanban has a column per stage: Backlog, In Sprint, In Progress, Ext. Blocked, In Review, Approved, Delivered, Done. Each card shows its ID (for example T-001), type, title, product, owner and due date (amber when close, red when overdue). Drag a card to move it; you can only make the moves your role allows, and an illegal drop snaps back. A Table view, a person filter, and a / search are also there.

Working a task (the side panel)

Click a task to open its panel. From here you (depending on role and stage):

  • Assign: claim a task as owner, add yourself as a collaborator, or (lead/admin) set the owner.
  • Move stage: pick an allowed next stage; moving to Ext. Blocked or Abandoned needs a typed reason.
  • Submit for Review: add the deliverable link to send your work to a lead (moves it to In Review).
  • Review work (lead/admin): Approve it, or request a revision with feedback (sends it back to In Progress).
  • Deliver to the requester, or Mark Done; set priority and due date; add notes, attachments and comments.
ⓘ The flow in one line

A task goes Backlog → pulled into a sprint → a member takes it In Progress → submits for review → a lead approves the work → it’s delivered to the requester (who accepts, or it auto-accepts) → Done. A revision sends it back a step; Ext. Blocked parks it; Abandoned stops it. Big requests appear as sibling tasks like T-001/2.

chapters.title: Sprints
chapters.html:
Sprints is where leads plan the week’s work: pull tasks from the backlog into the active sprint, give them due dates, watch progress, and close the sprint when it ends. A sprint runs Thursday to Wednesday.

What it’s for
Planning and running the sprint.
Read or act?
Action: build and close sprints.
Who
Lead Admin
Cycle
Thursday to Wednesday (7 days).

Running a sprint

  1. Create the sprint (when none is active). The start date must be a Thursday; only one sprint runs at a time.
  2. Fill it from the backlog. Drag tasks from the Backlog panel into the Current Sprint panel; a prompt lets you set a due date within the sprint week. Drag a task back out to remove it.
  3. Watch progress. A header bar shows percent done and a day countdown; a 7-day timeline lays out tasks by due date.
  4. Close the sprint when the week is over. Any unfinished tasks become spillovers and a new sprint is created automatically.
ⓘ “Overdue: close sprint”

When the Wednesday end date passes, the header prompts you to close the sprint. Closing rolls the incomplete tasks forward as spillovers (marked on their cards) into the next sprint, so nothing is lost. Use the / search to find a task across the sprint and backlog.

parts.subtitle: The manager dashboard and the social content calendar.

chapters.title: Dashboard
chapters.html:
The Dashboard is the manager’s reporting view: output, workload and sprint health. Leads and admins use it to see what the team is producing and where the pressure is.

What it’s for
Team output and workload reporting.
Read or act?
Read; CSV export.
Who
Lead Admin
Scope
By sprint, by person.

The three sections

  • Summary cards: In Review, Overdue, Ext. Blocked, Completion % and Spillovers. Click a card to drill into that bucket of tasks.
  • Deliverables Output: a table of completed deliverables by type, viewable by date or by person, over a date range, with a CSV export.
  • Team Workload: each person’s tasks across the stages; a person’s total turns orange when they are carrying a lot, an overload signal.
ⓘ Slice it by sprint and person

Use the sprint selector and the person filter at the top to focus the whole dashboard. The summary cards are clickable shortcuts into the exact tasks behind each number, which is the quickest way to act on what the report shows.

chapters.title: Social
chapters.html:
Social is the team’s content calendar: plan posts across channels, group them into campaigns, and watch a health monitor for posts at risk. Everyone can view it; the brand team can create and edit.

What it’s for
Planning and tracking social posts.
Read or act?
View all; brand team edits.
Who
Requester Member Lead Admin
Tabs
Calendar · Campaigns · Monitor.

The three tabs

  • Calendar: a month grid of posts. A post moves through idea → draft → approved → published (or cancelled), and holds one or more channel variants (each with its caption and asset, published per channel). Create a post with a title, date and at least one variant.
  • Campaigns: group posts under a named campaign with a date range and a status (active, completed, archived).
  • Monitor: an At Risk list (overdue posts and ones missing assets within 24 hours) plus an 8-week cadence table per channel.
ⓘ Who can change what

Anyone can view the calendar, but only the brand team can create or edit posts and campaigns; moving a post to approved and deleting a post are lead/admin actions. The Monitor tab’s red badge is your early warning that a scheduled post still has no asset.

parts.subtitle: Managing roles, disciplines and ageing thresholds.

chapters.title: Settings
chapters.html:
Settings is the admin screen for managing the team: who has which role and discipline, and the ageing thresholds that drive the warning dots and the auto-accept of delivered work.

What it’s for
Roles, disciplines and ageing rules.
Read or act?
Action: manage people & thresholds.
Who
Admin
Drives
Auto-accept & ageing dots.

Team

The team table, grouped into Lead, Brand Team and Requesters, lists each person with a Role dropdown (admin, lead, member, requester) and a Discipline dropdown (designer, 3D, copywriter, photo/video, social, lead). Changes save inline.

Ageing thresholds

For each stage you set a Warning, Critical and Auto-close time in hours. These drive the colour of the ageing dots on task cards and, importantly, the time after which delivered work auto-accepts if the requester has not responded.

⚠ You cannot change your own role

Your own role dropdown is disabled, so an admin cannot accidentally lock themselves out; another admin must make that change. Because the ageing thresholds control auto-accept, adjust them deliberately: a short auto-close means delivered work closes itself sooner.
